author: Jakson Gudawela
headline: ADNOC, EGPC and Dragon Oil chiefs to open the GOTECH plenary
deck: GOTECH's opening plenary is drawn entirely from operators, which is unusual for a technical conference and says something about who sets the agenda.
excerpt: GOTECH's chief executive plenary is drawn from EGPC, ADNOC Onshore and Offshore, OiLSERV Kuwait, Dragon Oil, Sharjah National Oil Corporation and United Energy Group.
content:
The chief executive plenary opening GOTECH in Dubai at the end of September is composed of operators: the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation, ADNOC Onshore and ADNOC Offshore, OiLSERV Kuwait, Dragon Oil, Sharjah National Oil Corporation and United Energy Group, moderated by Carole Nakhle, chief executive of Crystol Energy.

The composition is worth noting because technical conference plenaries are frequently dominated by the service sector, whose commercial interest in appearing is more direct. A panel of national and regional operators is a different proposition: these are the organisations that set specifications, award contracts and decide which technologies get field trials.

The range within the group is wider than the shared label suggests. ADNOC Onshore and Offshore operate at a scale and technical sophistication comparable to any international major, with large capital programmes and an established supply chain. EGPC operates in a mature basin under different fiscal and currency conditions. Sharjah National Oil Corporation is a smaller emirate-level operator working assets that would be marginal within a larger portfolio. Dragon Oil and United Energy Group bring international portfolios with regional headquarters.

That spread maps onto the technical programme's tracks. A large operator with new capacity is interested in artificial intelligence for reservoir management and in carbon capture at scale. A smaller operator working mature assets cares about marginal economics, well intervention cost and squeezing recovery from existing infrastructure. Both sets of problems appear on the same programme, which is one of the arguments for a regional conference over a company technical day.

The service companies are present — Baker Hughes, SLB and Halliburton all appear on the programme — but positioned as contributors to technical sessions rather than as the voice of the plenary. Jennifer Miskimins attends as the SPE's 2026 president and Faye Gerard from the International Association of Oil and Gas Producers, giving the professional body and the safety and standards perspective.

For the Gulf supply chain the plenary composition is the practical reason to attend. An operator chief executive describing capital priorities in public is giving suppliers a read on where the next tranche of spend goes, and the difference between a large operator's greenfield programme and a smaller one's intervention budget determines entirely which suppliers should be listening.

The programme comprises 93 sessions across five concurrent rooms, including seven panel and plenary sessions, 52 technical sessions and 19 poster sessions. Speaker and session detail is taken from SPE's published programme. For suppliers, an operator plenary is also a rare chance to hear capital priorities described without a service company framing them first.
